content.title: 2025 High Blood Pressure Guideline
content.narrative_summary: This guideline replaces the 2017 AHA/ACC guideline for management of high blood pressure in adults. A comprehensive literature search from December 2023 to June 2024 identified clinical studies, reviews, and evidence on human subjects published since February 2015. The guideline is presented as a living document to update current practice for primary care and specialty clinicians managing hypertension.

content.title: WHAT IS NEW
content.narrative_summary: Table 1 highlights new and/or substantially revised practice-changing recommendations since the last iteration of the guideline and is not a comprehensive list of all updates. Some of these recommendations have corresponding footnotes not captured in this table.

recommendation_tables.title: Table 1: What Is New

rows.recommendation: Severe hypertension

In adults with resistant hypertension, screening for primary aldosteronism is recommended regardless of whether hypokalemia is present to increase rates of detection, diagnosis, and specific targeted therapy.

In adults with an indication for screening for primary aldosteronism, it is recommended to continue most antihypertensive medications (other than MRA) prior to initial screening to minimize barriers to or delays in screening.

In adults with or without hypertension, potassium-based salt substitutes can be useful to prevent or treat elevated BP and hypertension, particularly for patients in whom salt intake is related mostly to food preparation or flavoring at home, except in the presence of CKD or use of drugs that reduce potassium excretion where monitoring of serum potassium levels is indicated.

In adults with hypertension without clinical CVD but with diabetes or CKD or at increased 10-year CVD risk (ie, ≥7.5 % based on PREVENT), initiation of medications to lower BP is recommended when average SBP ≥130 mm Hg and average DBP ≥80 mm Hg to reduce the risk of CVD events and total mortality.

In adults with hypertension without clinical CVD and with estimated 10-year CVD risk <7.5 % based on PREVENT, initiation of medications to lower BP is recommended if average SBP remains ≥130 mm Hg or average DBP remains ≥80 mm Hg after a 3- to 6-month trial of lifestyle intervention to prevent target organ damage and mitigate further increases in BP.

In adults with diabetes and hypertension, ACEI or ARB are recommended in the presence of CKD as identified by eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or albuminuria ≥30 mg/g and should be considered when mild albuminuria (<30 mg/g) is present to delay progression of diabetes-related kidney disease.

For adult patients with acute spontaneous ICH who present with SBP between 150 and 220 mm Hg, it can be beneficial to immediately lower SBP to 130 to <140 mm Hg for at least 7 days after ICH to improve functional outcomes, but stop antihypertensive medications if SBP <130 mm Hg.

rows.recommendation: In adults with acute spontaneous ICH requiring acute BP lowering, careful titration to ensure smooth, nonlabile, and sustained control of BP, avoiding peaks and large variability in SBP, can be beneficial for improving functional outcomes.

In patients undergoing successful brain reperfusion with endovascular treatment for a large vessel occlusion, lowering SBP <140 mm Hg within the first 24 to 72 hours after reperfusion can worsen long-term functional outcome.
In adults with hypertension, a goal of <130 mm Hg SBP is recommended to prevent mild cognitive impairment and dementia.

Pregnant individuals with SBP ≥160 mm Hg or DBP ≥110 mm Hg confirmed on repeat measurement within 15 minutes should receive antihypertensive medication to lower BP to <160/<110 mm Hg within 30 to 60 minutes to prevent adverse events.

Pregnant individuals with chronic hypertension (defined as prepregnancy hypertension or SBP 140–159 mm Hg and/or DBP 90–109 mm Hg prior to 20 weeks gestation) should receive antihypertensive therapy to achieve BP <140/90 mm Hg to prevent maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality.
Individuals with hypertension who are planning a pregnancy or who become pregnant should be counseled about the benefits of low-dose aspirin to reduce the risk of preeclampsia and its sequelae.
Individuals with hypertension who are planning a pregnancy or who become pregnant should not be treated with atenolol, ACEi, ARB, direct renin inhibitors, nitroprusside, or MRA to avoid fetal harm.

In adults with resistant hypertension, a more detailed evaluation for secondary causes, to include careful review of all medications and removal of those with interfering effects on BP, is beneficial for lowering BP and simplifying treatment.
All patients with hypertension who are being considered for RDN should be evaluated by a multidisciplinary team with expertise in resistant hypertension and RDN.

For patients with hypertension for whom RDN is contemplated, the benefits of lowering BP and potential procedural risks compared with continuing medical therapy should be discussed as part of a shared decision-making process to ensure patients choose the therapy that meets their expectations.

For adults with severe hypertension (>180/120 mm Hg) who are hospitalized for noncardiac conditions without evidence of acute target organ damage, intermittent use of additional intravenous or oral antihypertensive medications are not recommended to acutely reduce BP.

section_headings: 3.2.2 White-Coat Hypertension and Masked Hypertension, and White-Coat Effect and Masked Uncontrolled Hypertension
content.narrative_summary: This section describes the complex interplay of behavioral, environmental, hormonal, and genetic influences on blood pressure (BP) across the lifespan. Dietary factors such as high sodium intake, low potassium intake, alcohol overuse, and low intake of fiber, calcium, magnesium, and plant protein influence BP. Weight gain, obesity, insulin resistance, sleep disturbances (eg, obstructive sleep apnea), psychosocial stressors, and reduced physical activity contribute to elevated BP. Emerging data implicate environmental toxins such as air pollution and heavy metals. BP is a highly heritable trait; while hundreds of genetic loci have been identified, they collectively explain less than 10% of BP variance, underscoring the role of other factors and gene–environment interactions.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for White-Coat Hypertension and Masked Hypertension, and White-Coat Effect and Masked Uncontrolled Hypertension

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults with untreated office SBP ≥ 130 mm Hg or DBP ≥ 80 mm Hg, and without office SBP ≥ 160 mm Hg or DBP ≥ 100 mm Hg, it is reasonable to exclude white-coat hypertension using out-of-office BP monitoring before a diagnosis of hypertension is made.1-5
2. In adults with white-coat hypertension or masked hypertension, out-of-office BP monitoring is reasonable to exclude transition to a diagnosis of sustained hypertension.6-8
3. In adults with apparent treatment-resistant hypertension on office BP, it is reasonable to exclude white-coat effect, a form of pseudoresistance, using out-of-office BP monitoring.9-12

4. In adults who are taking antihypertensive medication and have elevated office BP (office SBP ≥ 130 mm Hg or DBP ≥ 80 mm Hg) but do not have resistant hypertension or office SBP ≥ 160 mm Hg or DBP ≥ 100 mm Hg, it is reasonable to exclude white-coat effect using out-of-office BP monitoring.1,4,13
5. In adults with untreated office SBP < 130 mm Hg and DBP < 80 mm Hg, it may be reasonable to exclude masked hypertension using out-of-office BP monitoring.5,13-15

6. In adults who are taking antihypertensive medication and have office SBP < 130 mm Hg and DBP < 80 mm Hg, it may be reasonable to exclude masked uncontrolled hypertension using out-of-office BP monitoring.13-15

content.title: Primary Aldosteronism
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis defines primary aldosteronism as disorders of autonomous aldosterone overproduction leading to sodium retention, volume expansion, suppressed renin activity, increased potassium excretion, hypertension, and cardiovascular and kidney damage. Hypokalemia may be absent despite severe excess aldosterone. Two-thirds of cases are from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and one-third from unilateral aldosterone-producing lesions. Although primary aldosteronism affects 5–10% of hypertensive patients and up to 20% of those with resistant hypertension, screening rates are only 1–2%. The recommendation-specific supportive text highlights a 2-to-4-fold increased risk of heart failure, stroke, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, and kidney damage in primary aldosteronism compared with primary hypertension, and notes that targeted therapies (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists or adrenalectomy) can reduce organ damage.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Primary Aldosteronism

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults with hypertension, screening for primary aldosteronism is recommended in the presence of any of the following conditions to increase rates of detection, diagnosis, and specific targeted therapy: resistant hypertension (regardless of whether hypokalemia is present), hypokalemia (spontaneous or diuretic induced), OSA, incidentally discovered adrenal mass, family history of early-onset hypertension, or stroke at a young age (<40 years).
2. In adults with stage 2 hypertension, screening for primary aldosteronism may be considered to increase rates of detection, diagnosis, and specific targeted therapy.

3. In adults with an indication for screening for primary aldosteronism, use of plasma aldosterone, renin activity, and the plasma aldosterone to renin activity ratio is recommended for initial screening to assess if there is biochemical evidence of primary aldosteronism.

4. In adults with an indication for screening for primary aldosteronism, it is recommended to continue most antihypertensive medications (other than mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [MRAs]) prior to initial screening to minimize barriers to or delays in screening.

5. In adults with hypertension and a positive screening test for primary aldosteronism or continued suspicion for primary aldosteronism based on suppressed plasma renin or disproportionate target organ damage, referral to a hypertension specialist or endocrinologist is recommended for further evaluation and treatment.

content.narrative_summary: This section defines obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) as a chronic condition with recurrent upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to hypoxia and disrupted sleep. content.title: 4. PREVENTION STRATEGIES
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes that primary hypertension arises from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, lifestyle choices, and chronic stress, and that healthy lifestyle behaviors—weight loss for those with overweight or obesity, a heart-healthy DASH diet, limiting sodium intake, increasing dietary potassium, engaging in aerobic and resistance exercise, and stress management—can prevent hypertension; alcohol intake is associated with higher SBP even in individuals without hypertension.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Lifestyle and Psychosocial Approaches

rows.recommendation: In adults who have overweight or obesity, weight loss is recommended with a goal of at least 5% of body weight reduction to prevent or treat elevated BP and hypertension.
In adults with or without hypertension, a heart-healthy eating pattern, such as the DASH eating plan, is recommended to prevent or treat elevated BP and hypertension.
In adults with or without hypertension, reduction of dietary sodium intake is recommended to <2,300 mg/d, moving toward an ideal limit of <1,500 mg/d to prevent or treat elevated BP and hypertension.

In adults with or without hypertension, potassium-based salt substitutes can be useful to prevent or treat elevated BP and hypertension, particularly for patients in whom salt intake is related mostly to food preparation or flavoring at home, except in the presence of CKD or use of drugs that reduce potassium excretion where monitoring of serum potassium levels is indicated.

In adults with elevated BP or hypertension, moderate potassium supplementation, ideally from dietary sources, is recommended to prevent or treat elevated BP and hypertension, except in the presence of CKD or use of drugs that reduce potassium excretion where monitoring of serum potassium levels is indicated.

Adults with or without hypertension who currently consume alcohol should be advised to pursue a recommended goal of abstinence, or at least to reduce alcohol intake to ≤1 drink/d for women and ≤2 drinks/d for men to prevent or treat elevated BP and hypertension.

In adults with or without hypertension, increasing physical activity, through a structured exercise program that includes aerobic exercise and/or resistance training, is recommended to prevent or treat elevated BP and hypertension.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of lifestyle and stress‐reduction interventions for hypertension. content.narrative_summary: The page provides supportive text for initial therapy: the primary goal is to reduce BP to target considering CVD risk and indications. content.title: 5.2.5. Antihypertensive Medication Adherence Strategies
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses evidence that single-pill combinations (SPCs) improve adherence and blood pressure lowering compared with equivalent free-pill combinations, with observational studies showing fewer cardiovascular events and deaths. Low-dose combinations of 3–4 drugs reduce BP more effectively than monotherapy over 3–6 months, though CVD outcomes were not evaluated. Initial two-drug combination therapy is reasonable for stage 2 hypertension, with cautious initiation in older adults due to hypotension risk. SPCs are cost-effective and allow longer follow-up, but may not be available in all dose combinations, in which case separate agents may be equally efficient. Most patients with stage 2 hypertension require at least two drug classes; a step-care approach (single-agent initiation and sequential titration) is reasonable for stage 1 hypertension, especially in older adults or those with hypotension history. Simultaneous administration of two RAS blockers (eg, ACEi plus ARB or renin inhibitor) or agents with similar mechanisms should be avoided due to increased CVD, kidney disease, and hyperkalemia risks. The synopsis notes that up to 50% of patients do not adhere to antihypertensive medications after one year; adherence can be assessed by self-report, questionnaires, prescription refills, pill counts, electronic monitoring, and chemical testing. It can be divided into initiation, persistence/implementation, and avoiding permanent discontinuation. Factors contributing to poor adherence include social determinants of health, poor health literacy, stress, anxiety, and depression.

Recommendations for Hypertension Treatment in Patients With CKD
content.narrative_summary:
Aortic Disease synopsis: Hypertension is a major risk factor for thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection, with each 10-mm Hg rise in BP increasing aneurysm rupture risk by about 30%. Intensive BP control (<130/80 mm Hg) is important for cardiovascular risk reduction in patients with hypertension and aortic disease, though optimal antihypertensive choice is extrapolated from acute aortic syndrome management and data are limited. See other sections of the 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease guideline for more detail.  

CKD synopsis: Hypertension affects 67%–92% of people with CKD and significantly raises CVD risk. Intensively lowering SBP to <130 mm Hg (mean achieved 121 mm Hg vs standard 136 mm Hg in SPRINT) reduces CVD events and mortality, including in CKD. An ACE inhibitor or ARB is recommended as initial therapy in CKD with moderate to severe albuminuria (≥30 mg/g) and may be considered in lower albuminuria based on expert opinion; similar recommendations apply in nondialysis CKD and early-stage dialysis.

content.title: 5.3.9.2. Acute Ischemic Stroke
content.narrative_summary: The preceding discussion describes that aggressive BP lowering (SBP <130 mm Hg) after intracerebral hemorrhage improved 90-day outcomes in INTERACT-2 and ATACH-2 trials but may be harmful at very low SBP; increased SBP variability in the first 24 hours is associated with worse disability and death. There is limited evidence guiding agent choice in the hyperacute ICH phase; IV nicardipine and other rapid‐onset, short-duration antihypertensives are appropriate, whereas venous vasodilators may be harmful. Meta-analysis suggests titratable agents, CCBs, and adrenergic blockers yield favorable outcomes vs fixed agents, RAS blockers, nitrates, or magnesium. Post hoc data support modest SBP lowering (160–180 mm Hg) in patients presenting with markedly high SBP (>220 mm Hg).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Acute Ischemic Stroke

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with acute ischemic stroke, hypotension and hypovolemia should be corrected to maintain systemic perfusion levels necessary to support organ function.

2. Patients who have elevated BP and are otherwise eligible for treatment with IV thrombolytics should have their BP lowered to SBP <185 mm Hg and DBP <110 mm Hg before IV thrombolytic therapy is initiated and should be maintained below 180/105 mm Hg for at least the first 24 hours after initiating thrombolytic therapy to avoid complications.

3. In patients who undergo endovascular treatment, it is reasonable to maintain the BP at ≤180/105 mm Hg during and for 24 hours after the procedure to improve long-term functional outcomes and prevent death.

4. In patients with BP of ≥220/120 mm Hg who did not receive IV thrombolytic or endovascular treatment and have no comorbid conditions requiring acute antihypertensive treatment, it might be reasonable to lower BP by 15% during the first 24 hours after onset of stroke to improve outcomes.

5. In patients with BP <220/120 mm Hg who do not receive IV thrombolysis or endovascular treatment and do not have a comorbid condition requiring urgent antihypertensive treatment, initiating or reinitiating treatment of hypertension within the first 48 to 72 hours after an acute ischemic stroke is not effective to prevent death or disability.

content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: High blood pressure occurs in up to 80% of acute ischemic stroke patients. While controlling BP may enhance cerebral perfusion and minimize edema and hemorrhagic transformation, rapid reduction even within the hypertensive range can be detrimental. Treatment decisions depend on IV thrombolysis, endovascular thrombectomy with successful reperfusion, very high BP (SBP ≥220 mm Hg or DBP ≥120 mm Hg), and comorbid conditions; for other patients, the benefit of early BP lowering is uncertain. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text: The optimal BP level for best outcomes in acute ischemic stroke is unknown. Observational studies conflict regarding lower BP and outcomes, and no trials address very low BP. RCTs of IV alteplase targeted SBP <185/110 mm Hg; meta-analyses suggest higher hemorrhage risk with higher BP, and ENCHANTED showed no clear benefit of targeting SBP 130–140 mm Hg. Higher BP after thrombectomy is linked to worse functional outcomes. Patients with severe hypertension (SBP/DBP >220/120 mm Hg) were excluded from trials; rapid BP reduction benefits are unproven and management should be individualized. No data favor one strategy of BP lowering over another after acute ischemic stroke.

content.narrative_summary: Section 5.5.1 defines gestational hypertension as new onset of hypertension after 20 weeks’ gestation without proteinuria or target‐organ damage, noting its association with maternal and fetal/neonatal adverse events and up to 30% progression to preeclampsia. High‐quality RCT data demonstrate that tighter diastolic blood pressure targets (85 vs 100 mm Hg) reduce severe maternal hypertension without increasing other adverse outcomes, and ACOG recommends managing severe‐range pressures (SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 mm Hg) similarly to preeclampsia. Section 5.5.2 describes preeclampsia as a multisystem inflammatory syndrome with hypertension and proteinuria or organ dysfunction, noting 20–50% of those with chronic hypertension develop superimposed preeclampsia, and highlights HELLP syndrome, eclampsia, and the role of magnesium sulfate and low‐dose aspirin. Section 5.5.3 emphasizes individualized postpartum blood pressure measurement and medication titration, advocating home blood pressure monitoring within 3–10 days of discharge, team‐based telehealth self‐management, and remote strategies to improve postpartum cardiovascular outcomes.

content.title: 6. COMPLICATIONS OF MANAGEMENT
content.narrative_summary: The page provides a synopsis of emerging evidence comparing intensive versus standard blood pressure (BP) therapy in adults with orthostatic hypotension (OH), noting OH prevalence, associated cardiovascular risks, and the rationale for screening and monitoring OH before and during antihypertensive treatment. Recommendation-specific supportive text summarizes analyses from large randomized trials showing that intensive BP lowering does not increase harm from OH, does not alter cardiovascular or mortality benefits regardless of OH status, and highlights the importance of assessing OH prior to initiating or intensifying therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of OH

rows.recommendation: In adults with hypertension, improved BP control is recommended to reduce the risk for OH.
In adults receiving intensive BP-lowering therapy with asymptomatic OH, treatment with a goal of SBP <130 mm Hg is reasonable due to increased CVD and mortality benefit.
In adults with hypertension initiating treatment or adding medication with a goal of SBP <130 mm Hg, assessment for symptomatic OH is reasonable to detect other chronic conditions.

content.title: 6.2. Hypertensive Emergencies and Severe Hypertension in Nonpregnant and Nonstroke Patients
section_headings: 6.2. Hypertensive Emergencies and Severe Hypertension in Nonpregnant and Nonstroke Patients
content.narrative_summary: Hypertensive emergencies carry high in-hospital and 1-year cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, with acute target organ damage such as pulmonary edema, neurologic deficits, acute kidney injury, or aortic dissection. Immediate, controlled blood pressure reduction is required to prevent further damage, while avoiding overly rapid correction in patients with chronic hypertension to prevent hypoperfusion. Patients without evidence of acute target organ damage (“hypertensive urgency”) should not receive aggressive parenteral therapy; instead, oral antihypertensive medications can be reinstated or intensified, preferably in the outpatient setting.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Hypertensive Emergencies and Severe Hypertension in Nonpregnant and Nonstroke Patients*

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults with a hypertensive emergency (BP >180 and/or >120 mm Hg and evidence of acute target organ damage), admission to an intensive care unit is recommended for continuous monitoring of BP and target organ damage and for consideration of parenteral administration of appropriate therapy (Tables 26 and 27, Figure 9).

2. For adults with a hypertensive emergency related to a compelling condition (eg, acute aortic syndrome or acute aortic dissection), SBP should be reduced to <140 mm Hg for most conditions and to <120 mm Hg in aortic dissection during the first hour, while monitoring for other target organ dysfunction.

3. For adults with a hypertensive emergency but without a compelling condition, SBP should be reduced with oral or parenteral therapy by no more than 25% within the first hour; then, if stable, to <160/100 mm Hg within the next 2 to 6 hours; and then cautiously to 130 to 140 mm Hg during the next 24 to 48 hours to limit target organ injury.

4. For adults with severe hypertension (>180/120 mm Hg) who are hospitalized for noncardiac conditions without evidence of acute target organ damage, intermittent use of additional IV or oral antihypertensive medications are not recommended to acutely reduce BP.

content.narrative_summary: Paragraphs 2–4 discuss the lack of randomized trial evidence comparing acute BP‐lowering strategies in most hypertensive emergencies aside from stroke/ICH, observational data linking higher SBP to increased complications (eg, aortic dissection), and endorsed SBP targets (eg, <130 mm Hg in aortic dissection). Pheochromocytoma hypertensive crisis is noted as requiring prompt BP reduction but not to <120–140 mm Hg immediately due to cardiovascular risks. Small trials in acute heart failure suggest a 15% SBP reduction in 30 minutes is safe, with more conservative 25% reduction in the first hour and gradual decreases thereafter. Extreme caution is advised in hospitalized patients with asymptomatic severe hypertension due to high rates of spontaneous BP falls and associations with worse outcomes; careful monitoring and avoidance of as-needed medications is recommended.

content.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Severe Hypertension and Hypertensive Emergency
content.narrative_summary: Flowchart outlining evaluation and management of patients with systolic blood pressure >180 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure >120 mm Hg, distinguishing hypertensive emergency (acute target organ damage) from severe hypertension without organ damage, with corresponding admission, treatment targets, and follow-up intervals. Recommendations are annotated by Class of Recommendation.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: FIGURE 9
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Severe Hypertension and Hypertensive Emergency
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Start with SBP >180 mm Hg or DBP >120 mm Hg. If acute target organ damage is present, classify as hypertensive emergency: admit to ICU (COR 1), then assess for aortic dissection or pheochromocytoma crisis. For aortic dissection, reduce SBP to <120 mm Hg (COR 1); for pheochromocytoma crisis, reduce SBP to <140 mm Hg in the first hour (COR 1). If neither, reduce SBP by 25% in the first hour to 160/100–110 and to normal over the next 24–48 hours (COR 1), and avoid parenteral BP lowering or intensified oral therapy in the acute setting (COR 3–Harm). If no organ damage (severe hypertension), identify setting: in ED, evaluate inpatient vs outpatient treatment based on indications beyond BP alone; in outpatient, no need to refer to ED—reinstitute, intensify, or modify therapy—and schedule close follow-up in 4 weeks. Legend indicates color coding of COR classes.

content.narrative_summary: Section 6.2.1 emphasizes rapid recognition and knowledge of specific treatment approaches for hypertensive emergencies, referencing Sections 6.2 and 5.3.9 and Tables 26 and 27 for preferred agents. Section 6.3 discusses the frequency and definition of sexual dysfunction in patients with hypertension, its assessment using validated tools, shared mechanistic pathways with vascular impairment, and the contribution of antihypertensive medications—particularly diuretics and most β-blockers—to sexual dysfunction. ARBs are noted to have a favorable profile. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors are considered safe and effective when coadministered except with CYP3A4 inhibitors or nitrates due to hypotension risk.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Patients Scheduled for Surgical Procedures

rows.recommendation: In patients with hypertension scheduled for major surgery who have been on BBs chronically, BBs should be continued throughout the perioperative period to assist with BP control.1-5
In patients with hypertension scheduled for elective major surgery, it is reasonable to continue most medications for hypertension throughout the perioperative period.
In patients with hypertension scheduled for major surgery, discontinuation of ACEi or ARB preoperatively may be considered to prevent hypotension during surgery.6-10

In patients scheduled for elective major surgery with SBP ≥180 mm Hg or DBP ≥110 mm Hg, deferring surgery may be considered especially in high-risk patients to minimize perioperative complications.11-13
In patients with hypertension scheduled for surgery, abrupt preoperative discontinuation of BB or clonidine may result in rebound hypertension and is potentially harmful.14
For patients with hypertension scheduled for surgery, BB should not be started on the day of surgery in BB-naïve patients because of increased risk of postoperative mortality.4,15,16

content.narrative_summary: The ‘Synopsis’ describes that perioperative hypertension increases cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk and bleeding, correlates with severity of hypertension, and that abrupt discontinuation of certain agents (e.g., beta-blockers, clonidine) may lead to rebound hypertension. It emphasizes assessing factors such as volume status, pain control, oxygenation, and bladder distention when considering pharmacologic BP control and refers to the 2024 perioperative cardiovascular management guideline for detailed noncardiac surgery recommendations. Under ‘Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text,’ it outlines: (1) continuation of beta-blockers if well tolerated, supported by observational studies; (2) expert‐opinion support for achieving guideline BP targets (<130/80 mm Hg) using oral or IV medications, with caution in patients at risk for perioperative hypotension (e.g., low BP, older adults); (3) mixed observational evidence regarding perioperative continuation versus discontinuation of ACE inhibitors/ARBs; and (4) conflicting data on delaying surgery for DBP >110 mm Hg, associations between preoperative hypertension and increased cardiovascular/cerebrovascular complications, and a recommendation to use baseline ambulatory BP to guide management.
